competency.competency_text: Recognise continuities in culture, tradition and civilisational values through political change

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace how cultural and civilisational ideas persisted across political change and explain the role they played in building collective confidence
assessment_items.question_text: Bande Mataram was composed by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay in 1875, set to music by Rabindranath Tagore, sung at the 1896 Calcutta Congress session, and adopted as India's National Song by the Constituent Assembly in 1950. Vivekananda's birthday (12 January) is observed as National Youth Day. What do these continuities demonstrate about the relationship between cultural ideas and political change?

options.label: A
options.text: Cultural ideas from the nineteenth century became frozen and were preserved unchanged into independent India without any political transformation.

options.label: B
options.text: Cultural ideas generated before formal political organisations existed persisted through the independence movement and were adopted by the new nation, showing that civilisational confidence outlasted and shaped political change.

options.label: C
options.text: The adoption of Bande Mataram and the National Youth Day shows that the Constituent Assembly rejected European models of nationhood in favour of religious tradition.

options.label: D
options.text: Vivekananda and Bankim Chandra were conscious political strategists who composed their works specifically to serve the future Congress's needs.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Misreads 'continuity' as 'frozen preservation'; misses that the ideas were actively adopted and given new political meaning at each stage.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Misreads the adoption of Bande Mataram as a rejection of European models; the chapter presents it as a civilisational affirmation, not an anti-European religious act.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Anachronistically projects political strategy onto figures who worked decades before the Congress existed; misses that the chapter presents their influence as unplanned cultural groundwork.

competency.competency_text: Recognise continuities in culture, tradition and civilisational values through political change

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace how a civilisational image of the motherland was adapted across regions and languages to serve a modern political cause
assessment_items.question_text: The image of 'Bharat Mata' appeared in Abanindranath Tagore's 1905 painting in Bengal, in Subramania Bharati's Tamil translation of Bande Mataram and his poems calling on Mother India to rise in the Madras presidency, and in Lala Lajpat Rai's Punjab publication titled Vande Mataram. What does the spread of this image across regions and languages demonstrate?

options.label: A
options.text: A civilisational image of India as a divine mother, originating in Bengali literature, was independently adopted and adapted across regions and languages, demonstrating the idea's capacity to carry nationalist meaning beyond its original context.

options.label: B
options.text: Because Bharati translated Bande Mataram into Tamil, the image was confined to regions where the Tamil version circulated and did not reach Hindi-speaking areas.

options.label: C
options.text: The Bharat Mata image was a top-down campaign organised by the Congress to create a unified national symbol.

options.label: D
options.text: The spread of Bharat Mata imagery shows that the independence movement was primarily religious rather than political in character.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Imposes an organisational structure that did not exist; the chapter presents the spread as independent adoption, not a centrally directed campaign.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses a religious image being used for political purposes with the movement being primarily religious; the chapter is explicit that the motherland imagery served a political nationalist function.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Contradicts the chapter's evidence — Lala Lajpat Rai's Punjab publication was titled Vande Mataram, extending the image to a very different region and language context.

competency.competency_text: Recognise and analyse manifestations of prejudice and discrimination in society

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify specific colonial policies as manifestations of systematic racial discrimination and explain the mechanisms by which they operated
assessment_items.question_text: After 1858, Indians in the army and civil services received lower pay than British counterparts; British-majority juries were lenient toward European crimes; Indians were excluded from clubs, trains and public spaces; the 1878 Arms Act barred Indians from keeping arms; and the 1878 Vernacular Press Act censored the Indian-language press. What do these policies have in common that makes them manifestations of systematic racial discrimination rather than isolated administrative decisions?

options.label: A
options.text: Each policy maintained a legal or institutional hierarchy in which Indians were subordinated to British interests in a different sphere — economic, legal, physical and informational — together forming a structure of racial control.

options.label: B
options.text: Each policy targeted a different group of Indians — soldiers, litigants, civilians, press readers — so they cannot be described as a single system.

options.label: C
options.text: They were all passed in the same year (1878) and were therefore a coordinated legislative programme against Indians.

options.label: D
options.text: They were manifestations of discrimination only because Indians protested them — if Indians had accepted them, they would have been neutral administrative rules.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Focuses on the coincidental date of two of the acts and misses that the exclusion from clubs, lower pay and biased juries predated 1878 — the system was not created by those two acts alone.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Mistakes targeting of different groups for lack of a common system; misses that the chapter's argument is precisely that the different spheres (economic, legal, physical, informational) together formed a unified structure of racial hierarchy.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Makes discrimination contingent on protest rather than on the nature of the policies themselves; this is a misconception about what discrimination means as a concept.

competency.competency_text: Recognise and analyse manifestations of prejudice and discrimination in society

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate two contrasting strategies for securing political voice for a discriminated group and explain the reasoning each strategy rested on
assessment_items.question_text: B.R. Ambedkar argued that separate electorates were the only way to secure genuine political voice for the Depressed Classes, because joint electorates would allow the Hindu majority to elect representatives from the Depressed Classes who were acceptable to the majority rather than truly representative of that community. Gandhi opposed separate electorates, fearing they would permanently divide Hindu society. Which evaluation of these two positions is best supported by the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: Ambedkar's position was correct because the Poona Pact failed to deliver genuine representation and the Depressed Classes remained politically voiceless after 1932.

options.label: B
options.text: Both positions rested on legitimate reasoning about different things: Ambedkar focused on the adequacy of representation for a discriminated group; Gandhi focused on the unity of the Hindu community — the Poona Pact was a compromise that addressed the immediate crisis without resolving the underlying disagreement.

options.label: C
options.text: Gandhi's position was correct because the Poona Pact resolved the dispute successfully and Ambedkar accepted reserved seats as an adequate alternative.

options.label: D
options.text: Neither position was genuinely concerned with the Depressed Classes — both Gandhi and Ambedkar were using the dispute as a platform for their own political influence.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Reads Ambedkar's acceptance of the Poona Pact as endorsement of its adequacy; misses that the chapter describes Ambedkar as someone who had himself suffered discrimination and whose concern about representation was principled, not surrendered.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reads the Poona Pact as a complete failure; misses that the chapter describes it as increasing the number of reserved seats — a concrete gain — even if the fundamental question of independent electoral power was unresolved.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Attributes cynical motive to both figures without textual support; the chapter presents both as genuinely concerned with the issue, differing on the best solution.

competency.competency_text: Analyse the relationship between production, consumption, trade and economic institutions

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how a colonial commodity monopoly and its taxation became the site of political resistance and mass mobilisation
assessment_items.question_text: Gandhi chose salt for the 1930 Civil Disobedience Movement because the colonial government held a monopoly on salt production and taxed it heavily. The Salt March was a 380-km walk to Dandi where Gandhi symbolically collected salt. Why was salt — rather than another colonial economic grievance — a particularly effective site for mass resistance?

options.label: A
options.text: Salt was a universal basic necessity consumed by every Indian regardless of region, caste or income, and its monopoly and taxation therefore affected the poorest Indians most directly — making resistance to it a genuinely mass act.

options.label: B
options.text: Salt was chosen because it had a long history in Indian religious ritual and therefore carried symbolic weight that other commodities lacked.

options.label: C
options.text: Salt was chosen because it was produced only in coastal Gujarat, making Dandi a geographically convenient destination for Gandhi's march from Sabarmati.

options.label: D
options.text: Salt was chosen because the colonial monopoly on salt was the largest single source of revenue for the British government, so attacking it would cause the greatest economic damage.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Reduces the choice to geographic convenience; misses the chapter's argument about universal necessity and the tax's disproportionate impact on the poor.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Focuses on revenue damage rather than the chapter's argument about mass inclusion; the chapter does not claim the salt tax was the largest revenue source — it says the monopoly and tax made salt a grievance that reached every Indian.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Introduces a religious-ritual argument the chapter does not make; the chapter's explanation is economic and political — universal necessity plus colonial monopoly and taxation.

competency.competency_text: Analyse the relationship between production, consumption, trade and economic institutions

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how the rejection of foreign goods and support for Indian enterprise functioned simultaneously as economic strategy and political resistance
assessment_items.chapter_section: The 1905 Partition of Bengal and National Awakening
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter notes that Swadeshi was not new in 1905: Jamsetji Tata founded Swadeshi Mills in Bombay in 1886, the Punjab National Bank was founded with Indian capital in Lahore in 1895, and Prafulla Chandra Ray founded Bengal Chemicals and Pharmaceuticals Ltd in 1901. After 1905, Swadeshi became a mass movement of boycotting foreign goods and promoting Indian-spun cloth. What does comparing the pre-1905 and post-1905 Swadeshi tell us about the relationship between economic practice and political resistance?

options.label: A
options.text: Economic self-reliance through Indian enterprise existed as a practice before it became a mass political weapon; the 1905 Partition gave an already-existing economic idea a political mobilising force it had not previously carried.

options.label: B
options.text: Pre-1905 Swadeshi enterprises were failures that the 1905 movement tried to revive by making Indian goods compulsory through boycott.

options.label: C
options.text: Swadeshi was always political — Jamsetji Tata, Lala Lajpat Rai and Prafulla Chandra Ray founded their enterprises specifically to support the Congress's nationalist programme.

options.label: D
options.text: The pre-1905 enterprises were purely commercial ventures with no connection to nationalism; Swadeshi became political only after 1905 when the Congress adopted it.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Misreads the pre-1905 enterprises as failures; the chapter presents them as successful precedents that demonstrated Indian economic capacity before the political movement adopted the idea.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Draws a sharp line between commercial and political that the chapter's logic does not support; the chapter's point is that the same practice carried different weight at different moments, not that it was purely commercial before 1905.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Anachronistically projects the 1905 mass movement back onto ventures founded between 1886 and 1901; Lajpat Rai was among the Punjab National Bank's founding directors, but the chapter does not say any of these were founded to support a Congress programme that did not yet exist in that form.

competency.competency_text: Appreciate India's contributions to world civilisation and democratic thought

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how India's civilisational heritage was articulated as a source of national confidence and international standing
assessment_items.question_text: Swami Vivekananda made a 'powerful defence of India's civilisation' at the 1893 Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago. He also founded the Ramakrishna Mission combining spiritual practice with social service, encouraged science and advised Jamsetji Tata in a way that led to the Indian Institute of Science, while rejecting blind imitation of the West. What did Vivekananda's position demonstrate about India's civilisational contribution to the world?

options.label: A
options.text: Vivekananda argued that India's spiritual tradition was superior to Western science and that India should reject Western knowledge entirely.

options.label: B
options.text: Vivekananda demonstrated that India's civilisational heritage — combining spiritual depth, social service and openness to science — offered the world a perspective that was neither inferior nor simply imitative of the West.

options.label: C
options.text: Vivekananda's Chicago address was significant mainly because it made Westerners aware of Hinduism for the first time, and this had no connection to Indian nationalism.

options.label: D
options.text: Vivekananda's contribution was primarily organisational — the Ramakrishna Mission's social service work was his main legacy rather than any ideas about civilisation.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Misreads Vivekananda's position as anti-Western; the chapter explicitly says he encouraged science and advised Tata on what became the Indian Institute of Science — he rejected blind imitation, not Western knowledge itself.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reduces Vivekananda's significance to organisational work; misses that the chapter presents his ideas about India's civilisation as the core of his contribution to nationalist confidence.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Treats the Chicago address as an informational event with no nationalist dimension; misses the chapter's argument that it gave Indians a basis for civilisational confidence vis-à-vis the colonial power.
